Dear Chairs and Reviewers,

We would like to express our sincere gratitude to all the chairs and reviewers for the time and effort they devoted to evaluating our work. Below is a brief summary of the discussion and the clarifications we provided during the rebuttal period.

All reviewers have given positive scores to our paper. They described our work as **“a novel benchmark”** (Reviewer 2mBT), **“scalable and reproducible”** (Reviewer 4n2i), and **“commendable”** (Reviewer RHxQ). Our experiments were characterized as **“extensive”** (Reviewer R2mBT), **“impressive”** (Reviewer R79wn), **“comprehensive”** (Reviewer R4n2i), and **“carefully structured”** (Reviewer RHxQ), and the paper itself as **“well-written and clearly organized”** (Reviewer R2mBT).

During the rebuttal period, we fully addressed the concerns and suggestions raised by the reviewers. To demonstrate the reliability of the appearance-grading process, we added appearance scores from two additional strong multimodal graders—o3 and Claude-3.5-Sonnet—as well as from humans. The results show that the relative order of the appearance scores given by GPT-4o is reliable. We also evaluated two more models (Claude-3.5-Sonnet and DeepSeek-R1) with OpenHands and Aider, enriching the comparison between the frameworks. In addition, we ran WebGen-LM three times to compute standard errors, providing clearer insight into the statistical significance of the results.

All reviewers **acknowledged our rebuttal efforts** and expressed appreciation for our detailed responses and clarifications.

We are deeply grateful for the time and effort that the reviewers and chairs have devoted to our work. Their insightful comments and suggestions have been invaluable in improving our project.

Best regards,  
The Authors

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for the perceptive comments and useful suggestions. We address your concerns as follows:

**Q1.** One key recommendation for improvement is the inclusion of uncertainty metrics (e.g., standard errors) in the results tables and plots, providing readers with clearer insight into the statistical significance and variability of the results.

**A1.** Thank you for your insightful suggestion. To provide a clearer picture of the statistical significance and variability of our results, we tested WebGen-LM-32B, WebGen-LM-14B, and WebGen-LM-7B three times at a temperature of 0.5. The resulting scores, together with their standard errors, are reported in the tables below. The standard errors for the accuracy and appearance scores are all below 1.0 %, which is relatively low and indicates that our results are reliable. The standard errors for each category are slightly larger because the number of samples in each category is smaller, but they still fall within a reasonable range. These findings demonstrate that our benchmark is robust and can reliably reflect the performance of agent systems. We did not re-evaluate the other models multiple times during the rebuttal period because of limited time and budget, but we plan to add uncertainty metrics for all results in the future.
|Model|Yes Rate|Partial Rate|No Rate|Start Failed|Accuracy|Appearance Score|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|WebGen-LM-32B|34.0±0.8|8.5±0.4|57.1±0.6|0.4±0.7|38.2±0.8|2.8±0.0|
|WebGen-LM-14B|24.9±1.1|9.1±1.1|65.6±0.8|0.4±0.6|29.5±0.6|2.5±0.1|
|WebGen-LM-7B|24.5±1.1|7.1±0.6|68.3±0.7|0.1±0.1|28.0±0.9|2.5±0.0|


|Model|Content Presentation|User Interaction|Data Management|Functional Testing|Data Display Testing|Design Validation Testing|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|WebGen-LM-32B|46.6±1.8|34.2±2.6|37.0±1.6|28.7±0.7|42.5±0.5|58.2±3.2|
|WebGen-LM-14B|31.6±1.4|27.4±1.1|31.3±0.6|22.5±1.4|27.8±0.8|51.5±2.1|
|WebGen-LM-7B|26.4±1.3|24.2±1.0|37.3±1.2|19.9±2.1|29.0±1.4|49.2±1.5|


**Q2.** Table 7 and Figure 3 present somewhat repetitive information and could be streamlined.

**A2.** Thank you for the valuable suggestion. Figure 3 presents a bar chart of the accuracies reported in Table 7, which we originally included to provide a straightforward visualisation of how accuracy improves as the training-data size increases. The information in the table and the figure is somewhat repetitive, so we will remove Figure 3 and retain only Table 7 in the revised paper.

**Q3.** The authors might consider a citing a somewhat relevant work that employs similar automated testing strategies in coding benchmarks, specifically related to version adaptation in software libraries, such as the study "GitChameleon: Unmasking the Version-Switching Capabilities of Code Generation Models"

**A3.** Thank you for the valuable suggestion. We will cite GitChameleon [1] in the revised paper and discuss its relation with our work. GitChameleon comprises 116 Python-based version conditioning problems. Similar to our work, GitChamelean uses unit tests to enable automated testing of the outputs generated by LLMs, though their tests are assertion-based while ours are based on GUI Agent operation results on the generated LLMs. In addition, [2] and [3] also uses assert-based unit tests for automated testing, which we will also cite and discuss in the revised paper.

[1] Islah, Nizar, et al. "GitChameleon: Unmasking the Version-Switching Capabilities of Code Generation Models." arXiv preprint arXiv:2411.05830 (2024).

[2] Chandel, Shubham, et al. "Training and evaluating a jupyter notebook data science assistant." arXiv preprint arXiv:2201.12901 (2022).

[3] Yuhang Lai, et al. “Ds-1000: A natural and reliable benchmark for data
 science code generation.” 18319–18345. PMLR (2023).

We appreciate your insightful feedback and valuable suggestions. Our responses to your concerns are presented below:

**Q1.** Instructions are derived from 20 predefined categories, which may not capture niche or emerging web applications. Crowdsourcing or iterative category expansion could address this.

**A1.** Thank you for the insightful suggestion. We will further increase the sample number and task diversity through crowdsourcing and iterative category expansion, enabling future versions of WebGen-Bench to capture niche and emerging web applications. 
To broaden task diversity, we will extend the 20 application categories presented in Appendix E. Following are six new categories that will be added  in a future version of WebGen-Bench. Additional categories will be added continuously as new web applications emerge. This discussion will be incorporated into the Limitations and Future Work section of the paper.
- Health & Wellness Tracking Apps: Applications for monitoring fitness metrics, nutrition, exercise routines, and overall wellbeing.
- Personal Finance & FinTech Apps: Platforms for budgeting, expense tracking, investments, digital wallets, and other financial services.
- Dating & Matchmaking Platforms: Services that facilitate user matching, communication, and relationship building.

Assistant:

User:

Assistant:  
*Adding the button and implementing export...*

Example of (2):

User:

Assistant:  
... Initial map with an ivory canvas and forest-green sidebar is ready.

User:

Assistant:  
... Chart library has been linked and a placeholder graphic inserted.

User:   
Please deliver the next update that completes those tasks:  
- When a neighborhood is clicked, its tooltip must list population, median income, and crime rate.  
- The bar chart must redraw with three bars in dark green that reflect the same values.  

Assistant:  
*I will implement the following requirments...*

Instructions to be filtered out:

"Please build me a single-page website for my startup, and make sure there’s also a separate blog page where I can publish articles."

Example 3: Overly Open-Ended Creative Request

"Please design a site that’s never been seen before. Just surprise me and make it unforgettable."

summary.value: This paper introduces WebGen-Bench, a novel benchmark focused on evaluating the ability of LLM-based agents to generate websites from scratch, with an emphasis on both functionality and aesthetic quality. The benchmark comprises 101 curated tasks and 647 test cases, validated through a combination of automated testing using the WebVoyager UI agent and manual review with GPT-4o. The authors also present WebGen-Instruct, a training dataset of 6.6k instructions, and demonstrate that fine-tuned models (WebGen-LM) outperform existing proprietary baselines. The benchmark is well-designed and practically valuable, addressing the current limitations of LLM-based code agents in building usable websites for non-expert users.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper proposes a novel benchmark that evaluates LLM-based agents on generating complete websites from natural language instructions. This task is significantly more challenging than traditional benchmarks focused on bug-fixing or patching, and it better reflects real-world scenarios involving non-expert users.
2. WebGen-Bench assesses both the functional correctness and visual appeal of the generated websites. This dual focus enables a more holistic evaluation of code agents.
3. The benchmark instructions are grounded in real-world demands, sourced from platforms like Upwork and Freelancer. The instruction formulation simulates user intents from non-programmers, making the benchmark highly relevant to the practical deployment of LLM-based coding agents.
4. The authors conduct extensive experiments across multiple frameworks and LLMs. They also introduce a 6.6k-scale instruction dataset (WebGen-Instruct) and fine-tune open-source models with transparent methods such as rejection sampling and appearance-based filtering, ensuring reproducibility and reliability.
5. The paper is well-written and clearly organized. Figures like the benchmark pipeline and evaluation examples are informative and effectively convey the benchmark structure, data composition, and evaluation strategy.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Although GPT-4o is prompted to rate website aesthetics, the paper lacks a systematic analysis of inter-rater consistency or human-grounded calibration. Since aesthetics can be subjective, using only a single model’s score may not reflect broader user preferences. Incorporating human evaluation or ensemble LLM ratings would strengthen the appearance assessment.
2. While the benchmark quantifies performance across multiple models and frameworks, the paper provides limited qualitative or categorical analysis of common failure patterns. More insights into the types of requirements (e.g., form logic, dynamic rendering) that models often fail to implement would help both researchers and practitioners target weaknesses more effectively.
3. While the test set covers diverse categories (101 tasks), some subcategories appear underrepresented. This limits statistical power when comparing performance across instruction types. A future version of WebGen-Bench could expand task diversity while maintaining evaluation cost-efficiency.

summary.value: This paper introduces a benchmark test named WebGen-Bench, which is used to evaluate the ability of agents based on large language models (LLMs) to generate interactive and functional websites from scratch. WebGen-Bench contains a diverse set of website generation instructions, co-created by human annotators and GPT-4o, covering most important types of web applications. The paper provides a comprehensive evaluation of three high-performance code agent frameworks—Bolt.diy, OpenHands, and Aider—using different proprietary LLMs as engines, demonstrating the challenges of the benchmark test.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The study introduces WebGen-Bench, the \textbf{first} benchmark for evaluating the ability of LLM-based agents to generate interactive and functional websites from scratch.
2. After fine-tuning based on the created training set, the performance of WebGen-LM is impressive.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The paper uses GPT-4o to evaluate the aesthetics of generated web pages, but it does not conduct experiments to align these evaluations with human aesthetic judgments.
2. The paper tests only Deepseek-V3 in OpenHands and Aider. To demonstrate WebGen-LM's good performance and robustness, it is recommended to also compare and evaluate WebGen-LM with other models within the OpenHands and Aider agent frameworks.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
Suggestions for Improvement：
The paper could enrich the experimental section by using a diverse range of models under different frameworks. This would not only verify the excellent performance of WebGen-LM but also demonstrate its robustness.

Questions：
In Table 4, GPT-4o's performance is significantly worse than that of other models. The paper should provide a more detailed explanation and discussion of this phenomenon, but it fails to do so. I want to know the reason for this phenomenon.

final_justification.value: The authors added results of  Claude-3.5-Sonnet and DeepSeek-R1. I keep my original positive score.

summary.value: The paper introduces WebGen-Bench, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of LLM-based agents to generate interactive and functional websites from scratch. The benchmark includes diverse instructions spanning three major categories (Content Presentation, User Interaction, Data Management) and 13 subcategories, ensuring comprehensive coverage of web application types. The authors also construct WebGen-Instruct, a training dataset with 6,667 instructions, and demonstrate that fine-tuning open-source models (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder-32B) on this dataset improves performance, achieving 38.2% accuracy—surpassing proprietary models like DeepSeek-R1. The use of automated testing via the WebVoyager UI agent and GPT-4o for appearance grading enhances reproducibility and scalability.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Novel Benchmark: Introduces WebGen-Bench for evaluating LLM-generated websites from scratch, with 101 diverse instructions and 647 test cases.
2. Training Dataset: Provides WebGen-Instruct, a decontaminated dataset of 6,667 instructions, enabling fine-tuning that boosts model performance beyond proprietary LLMs.
3. Automated Evaluation: Uses WebVoyager for functional testing and GPT-4o for appearance scoring, ensuring scalable and reproducible assessments.
4. Comprehensive Analysis: Evaluates 3 agent frameworks and 7 LLMs, revealing performance gaps and key failure modes in website generation.
5. Open & Reproducible: Publicly releases datasets, code, and model weights, supporting further research in LLM-based web development.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Instructions are derived from 20 predefined categories, which may not capture niche or emerging web applications. Crowdsourcing or iterative category expansion could address this. 
2. GPT-4o’s grading (1–5 scale) is subjective. Including human ratings or multi-model consensus (e.g., Claude + GPT) may help to reduce bias of single model.
3. The fine-tuning dataset (600 trajectories) is small. Scaling up with synthetic data or active learning might further improve the robustness of the model .
4. Generated websites average 315 LOC, which seems to be simpler than real industrial projects.
5. The existing instructions are static. Is it possible to combine iterative user feedback (for example, simulated "client" interaction) during the generation process to better simulate real development?

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: The rebuttal effectively resolved most of my concerns, therefore I raise my final rating.

summary.value: The paper introduces WebGen-Bench, a novel benchmark to evaluate the capabilities of LLM-based agents in generating complete websites from scratch, a domain that is highly relevant and ripe for automation. The authors present a comprehensive approach that includes dataset generation, practical testing mechanisms, and structured experiments, significantly advancing the evaluation of AI agents in software engineering. This benchmark specifically addresses the need for realistic, practical scenarios that closely mirror real-world use cases, focusing not only on functionality but also on usability and aesthetics, thus providing a well-rounded assessment tool for future research and development.

strengths_contributions.value:
Regarding dataset construction, the authors demonstrate commendable efforts by generating approximately 10,000 detailed project descriptions. Importantly, they ensure minimal contamination between the test and train datasets, an aspect crucial for a robust evaluation. The decision to minimize technical jargon within the instructions is particularly valuable, aligning the dataset closely with realistic, non-technical user scenarios.

A significant strength of the paper is its careful approach to testing. Instead of solely relying on potentially superficial evaluations by LLMs, the authors opt for a comprehensive, practical testing framework involving a UI-agent (WebVoyager). This method provides a more rigorous evaluation of website functionality. The alignment study further strengthens this evaluation, as does the thoughtful addition of assessing website appearance, offering a well-rounded benchmark.

The experiments are carefully structured, exploring multiple agent frameworks and integrating both open-source and proprietary models. These experiments not only validate the effectiveness of the training set but also illustrate the considerable challenge posed by the benchmark, as reflected in relatively modest performance outcomes.

limitations_weaknesses.value: One key recommendation for improvement is the inclusion of uncertainty metrics (e.g., standard errors) in the results tables and plots, providing readers with clearer insight into the statistical significance and variability of the results.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The dataset and code are accessible on HF and github respectively.

additional_feedback.value:
* Table 7 and Figure 3 present somewhat repetitive information and could be streamlined.

* The authors might consider a citing a somewhat relevant work that employs similar automated testing strategies in coding benchmarks, specifically related to version adaptation in software libraries, such as the study "GitChameleon: Unmasking the Version-Switching Capabilities of Code Generation Models"

N.B.: I use chatGPT to polish the review. The substance is however entirely human generated!

title.value: WebGen-Bench: Evaluating LLMs on Generating Interactive and Functional Websites from Scratch

abstract.value:
LLM‑based agents have demonstrated great potential in generating and managing code within complex codebases. In this paper, we introduce WebGen-Bench, a novel benchmark designed to measure an LLM-based agent's ability to create multi-file website codebases from scratch. It contains diverse instructions for website generation, created through the combined efforts of human annotators and GPT-4o. These instructions span three major categories and thirteen minor categories, encompassing nearly all important types of web applications.
To assess the quality of the generated websites, we generate test cases targeting each functionality described in the instructions. These test cases are then manually filtered, refined, and organized to ensure accuracy, resulting in a total of 647 test cases. Each test case specifies an operation to be performed on the website and the expected outcome of the operation.
To automate testing and improve reproducibility, we employ a powerful web-navigation agent to execute test cases on the generated websites and determine whether the observed responses align with the expected results.
We evaluate three high-performance code-agent frameworks—Bolt.diy, OpenHands, and Aider—using multiple proprietary and open-source LLMs as engines. The best-performing combination, Bolt.diy powered by DeepSeek-R1, achieves only 27.8\% accuracy on the test cases, highlighting the challenging nature of our benchmark.
Additionally, we construct WebGen-Instruct, a training set consisting of 6,667 website-generation instructions. Training Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct on Bolt.diy trajectories generated from a subset of the training set achieves an accuracy of 38.2\%, surpassing the performance of the best proprietary model.
We release our data-generation, training, and testing code, along with both the datasets and model weights at https://github.com/mnluzimu/WebGen-Bench.
